opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the teenager example is really striking to me. A teenager learns to drive in something like ten hours of practice, maybe twenty. That's a remarkably small amount of experience. And they don't come out of it with some brittle skill. They come out of it reasonably robust. They can handle situations they've never seen before.

What's interesting is what isn't happening there. Nobody is giving them a carefully designed reward signal for every second of driving. They're not doing millions of trials. Somehow they already have a sense of when they're doing well and when they're doing badly. You feel it. You feel unconfident when you take a turn too fast, you feel it's not right, and you correct. So there's some kind of internal value function that's already very good, and it lets them learn from very little external feedback.

You might say, well, that's just evolution. Evolution gave us priors for vision, for locomotion, for avoiding danger. And I think that's partly true. For things like vision and moving around, there's probably a lot that evolution has given us. But driving is not something evolution prepared us for. Neither is math, neither is coding. And yet people learn those things with this sample efficiency and this robustness too. So it suggests to me that it's not just a pile of task-specific priors. There's something about the learning itself, some more general mechanism, that is just better than what we have in our models today.

And I think that's one of the most important open questions. Our models are, in some ways, extremely impressive. They can do things on evals that look superhuman. But then they generalize dramatically worse than people. You see these strange failures that a human would never make. And the gap between how well a human generalizes from a small amount of experience and how our models generalize, that, to me, is the crux. If you could understand what's going on with the teenager, really understand it, I think that would be a very big deal.

r001.rationale: It says a teenager learns to drive with roughly ten or twenty hours of practice, calling that remarkably little experience.

r002.rationale: It describes the learner noticing when a turn is too fast, feeling unconfident, and correcting—learning signals that arise through driving.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the teenager example is really striking, and it's worth sitting with for a moment. A fifteen-year-old gets in a car, and within something like ten hours of practice, they're a competent driver. Not a great driver, but competent. They can handle a highway, they can merge, they can react to a kid running into the street. And they've never driven before. They have no driving data in the sense that we think about training data.

Now, if you look at what we do with self-driving cars, we have millions of hours of driving, far more than any human will ever experience, and the systems are getting good, but it took enormous amounts of data to get there. So the sample efficiency gap is huge. And I think the interesting question is, why?

One answer is that the teenager isn't actually starting from scratch. They've spent fifteen years looking at the world. They understand objects, they understand that cars don't pass through each other, they understand physics intuitively, they've been a passenger thousands of times. So there's this enormous prior. And then driving is a kind of fine-tuning on top of a very rich world model. That's part of it, and I think that's real.

But I don't think it's the whole story, because even when you account for the prior, the way the teenager learns from each experience is different. They make one mistake, they brake too late once, and they feel it, and they adjust. They don't need to see that situation ten thousand times. There's something about how humans extract the lesson from a single episode, and generalize it correctly, that we don't understand well and that our current methods don't replicate. Our models learn by seeing a very large number of examples and slowly shifting their weights. The teenager seems to be doing something more like reasoning about what went wrong and updating in a targeted way.

And the other thing I'd point to is that the teenager has a very good sense of what they don't know. When they get on the highway the first time, they're nervous, they're careful, they drive slowly. Their uncertainty is calibrated to their actual competence. And as they get experience, the confidence grows in step with the skill. Our models don't have that in the same way. They'll be equally confident in situations they've never encountered before.

So I'd say the distinctive thing is really these three together: a very deep prior about how the world works, extremely efficient learning from individual experiences, and a kind of self-awareness about the limits of your own ability. If you had to pick one problem to solve to get to something that learns like a human, I think it's the second one. The efficiency of learning from a small amount of experience. That's the thing that would change everything.

r001.rationale: It says a teenager becomes a competent driver after roughly ten hours of practice, contrasting this with the enormous data required by self-driving systems.

r002.rationale: It describes the teenager braking too late, feeling the result, and adjusting, showing learning from interaction with the car and environment.

astra-6.text:
What’s striking is how little experience a teenager needs to learn to drive. After a few dozen hours of practice, they can handle situations they’ve never encountered before. They still make mistakes, of course, but they’ve acquired something quite general.

Now, you could say: they’ve already had sixteen years of visual experience, of watching people move through the world, of learning about cause and effect. And that’s true. They’re not learning from scratch. But that’s also the interesting part. Their prior experience gives them something they can apply very efficiently to a new task.

So I think the question is: what is it about human learning that makes this possible? How do you get knowledge that transfers so well, such that a relatively small amount of practice produces a robust new capability? That seems like a very important property to understand.

r001.rationale: It says a teenager can learn to drive after only a few dozen hours of practice, identifying driving as a low-sample learning example.

r002.rationale: It mentions practice and prior visual experience, but does not clearly say the teenager derives a learning signal through interaction with the car and environment.

sol-6.1.text:
What strikes me is how little experience a teenager needs to learn to drive. They get some instruction, spend some hours practicing, and then they can handle situations they’ve never encountered before. They’re still going to make mistakes, but they have a remarkable ability to generalize.

And of course, they’re not starting from scratch. They’ve spent their whole life seeing the world, watching things move, understanding other people. So the question is: how do they take all that prior experience and turn it into a new skill so quickly? I think that’s a very important property of human learning.

r001.rationale: The response says a teenager needs only some instruction and a few hours of practice to learn to drive, communicating that relatively few samples are needed.

r002.rationale: The response mentions practicing and prior experience observing the world, but does not clearly state that the teenager derives a learning signal through interaction with the car and environment.
